references.text: God reveals himself with the name "I am" (אֲנִי יְהוָה), confirming his identity as the God of Israel.
God will bring Israel out of Egypt with great judgments (וּבִשְׁפָטִים גְּדֹלִים), fulfilled through the plagues.
Reference to God bringing Israel out of Egypt with a stretched-out arm (בִּזְרוֹעַ נְטוּיָה) and great judgments.
Reminder that Israel were slaves in Egypt and that the Lord brought them out with a strong hand and a stretched-out arm.
God saved (וְהִצַּלְתִּי) Israel from slavery in Egypt with a strong hand.
Confession that the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt with a strong hand, a stretched-out arm, and great judgments.
God redeemed (גָאַלְתָּ) his people with his arm, the children of Jacob and Joseph.
Praise song honoring God for bringing Israel out of Egypt with a strong hand and a stretched-out arm.
Prophetic prayer that the Lord's arm may act again as when he saved Israel from Egypt.
Jeremiah reminds that God brought Israel out of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and a stretched-out arm.
God revealed himself to Israel in Egypt and swore to bring them out to a land he had chosen for them.
Stephen's speech about how Moses led the people out and performed wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness.
Paul proclaims that the God of Israel exalted the people during their stay in Egypt and brought them out with an uplifted arm.
A direct theological parallel where 1 Samuel confirms and repeats God's saving act from Exodus as the basis for his relationship with Israel.
Highlights the connection between deliverance from Egypt and the status of being God's servants; freedom is the prerequisite for the new service.
The same event and motif (God's hand) showing that Israel's liberation is simultaneously a revelation of God's righteous judgment against Egypt.
Reuse of the identity formula showing that the memory of the exodus from Egypt is the foundation for both judgment and blessing.
Complementary parts of the same salvation plan: 3:10 is Moses' commission, while 6:6 is the message to the people about the same action.
A prophetic parallel where Ezekiel uses the exodus motif as a picture of the future restoration from captivity.
Repetition of a fundamental confession of faith: God's deliverance from Egypt is the absolute basis for his demand for holiness.
Expansion of the same event; Leviticus 26:13 elaborates on the meaning of 'great judgments' by describing the complete liberation from the yoke.
